items.title: Artificial intelligence ethical awareness and academic integrity among medical students at the University of Khartoum: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical education implies significant opportunities along with significant ethical challenges. Despite the substantial medical student uptake of artificial intelligence globally, little comprehensive assessments of ethical awareness are being conducted. This study aimed to assess artificial intelligence awareness and academic integrity level among University of Khartoum medical students and to examine relationships between the awareness level, demographic factors, artificial intelligence exposure, and tool use behavior. An institutional cross-sectional descriptive study of Years 3–6 medical students at University of Khartoum Faculty of Medicine in 2025 was conducted. A convenience sampling with quota allocation was used, and 349 students responded. The instrument included demographic variables, artificial intelligence exposure measures, and the 32-item Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity Scale. Nonparametric tests were applied. Participants were predominantly female (69.3%) with a mean age of 22.85 years. The median total Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity score was 4.16, indicative of moderate ethical awareness based on sample-derived empirical tertiles. Privacy and Data Protection were highest (median 4.67), with lowest scores in Transparency and Fairness/Non-Discrimination (3.80). Female students were more aware ( P = .01). No year-based differences observed. While 63.9% had minimal formal artificial intelligence exposure, 51.6% had moderate to high informal exposure. ChatGPT usage was prevalent (94.6%), and Google Gemini/Notebook LM usage was strongly associated with higher awareness ( P = .003). Informal exposure was positively correlated with awareness ( P = .01), but formal exposure was not. Multiple regression indicated that gender, informal exposure, and tool accounted for 11.2% of the variance in awareness. University of Khartoum medical students showed moderate-to-high aggregate artificial intelligence, ethical sensitivity, with areas of privacy protection and accountability being of particular strength. Gaps exist for awareness of transparency and fairness. The dominance of informal learning pathways over formal instruction, and gender variability favoring female students are significant findings. Findings highlight the need for institutional policies and conducting longitudinal research to track the evolution of AI ethics throughout medical training.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ACADEMIC WRITING: OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES, AND ETHICAL GUIDELINES FOR HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed academic writing, creating new opportunities for students, researchers, and university teachers. AI-powered applications can assist users in generating ideas, organizing arguments, improving grammar, expanding vocabulary, paraphrasing sentences, and editing academic texts. However, the integration of these technologies into higher education also raises important questions concerning academic integrity, authorship, originality, critical thinking, and the reliability of automatically generated information. This article examines the role of AI in academic writing, focusing on its educational benefits, methodological limitations, and ethical implications. The study employs a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach based on a review of relevant academic literature and international guidelines on generative AI in education and research. The analysis suggests that AI can support the development of academic writing when it is used as an assistive instrument rather than a substitute for independent intellectual work. Particular attention is paid to the responsibilities of students, researchers, and educational institutions in ensuring transparent and responsible AI use. The article argues that effective integration requires AI literacy, critical evaluation of generated content, appropriate disclosure practices, and assessment methods that recognize the importance of human reasoning. It concludes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on technological availability but on the principles governing its application in academic contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Alternative, Nonformal, and Adult Learning in the Global South: Protocol for a Mixed-Methods Systematic Review
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has expanded rapidly, yet it remains concentrated in higher education and formal schooling in high-income countries. Alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs, which serve out-of-school youth and adults across the Global South, are largely absent from this evidence base. No systematic synthesis has examined how AI is used in these programs, what outcomes it produces, and what conditions shape its adoption. Objective: This protocol describes a mixed-methods systematic review that will identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on AI use in alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for mixed-methods systematic reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-P. Searches will cover Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, four regional databases, and grey literature sources for studies published from January 2015 onward. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and appraise quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Quantitative findings will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with meta-analysis where at least three comparable studies exist. Qualitative findings will be synthesized thematically. Both strands will be integrated through a convergent segregated approach, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Discussion: The review will provide the first consolidated synthesis of AI use in second-chance and adult learning in the Global South. Its findings will inform program managers, teacher developers, and policymakers responsible for programs such as the Philippine Alternative Learning System (ALS). Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; nonformal education; adult learning; Alternative Learning System; Global South; systematic review protocol

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HEALTHCARE: ITS POTENTIALS AND RISKS
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into the clinic with remarkable speed. Machine learning systems now read medical scans, flag sepsis before symptoms declare themselves, draft clinical notes, and coach patients through their smartphones. This article examines the promise and the peril of this transformation in narrative form, and then applies the lens to a single, vivid case: the intertwined epidemics of sleep deprivation and migraine in young adults, where wearable sensors and predictive algorithms are beginning to change how these conditions are detected, studied, and managed. The evidence suggests that AI's greatest near-term contribution is not replacing clinicians but extending their reach — while its greatest dangers, including algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, data privacy erosion, and over-reliance, demand deliberate governance. The article argues that the future of medical AI will be decided less by the sophistication of the algorithms than by the wisdom of the humans who deploy them.

items.title: AUTOMATION OF JUDICIAL DECISIONS BY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ITS CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS
items.abstract: This article analyzes the constitutional limits of the automation of judicial decisions via Artificial Intelligence (AI), investigating its impact on the reasoning and impartiality of the Brazilian Judiciary. Faced with a litigation crisis and a massive volume of lawsuits, technology has been adopted to ensure procedural speed. However, the study examines the risks of automation bias and algorithmic opacity, which threaten to transform the law into a statistical system and undermine due process. Methodologically, the research is based on a review of literature and documents, grounded in legal doctrine and Resolution No. 332/2020 of the National Council of Justice (CNJ). The study argues that technological efficiency cannot supersede fundamental guarantees, making it imperative to maintain a "human reserve" at the core of the decision-making process. It concludes that AI should serve strictly as a tool for procedural management, preserving the human—and non-delegable—prerogative of the act of adjudication.

items.title: Being recognized as human by AI: algorithmic disrespect and the crisis of recognition in the digital age
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly does more than identify individuals; in many institutional contexts, it helps determine who is seen, trusted, and included. This paper argues that algorithmic systems increasingly participate in practices of social recognition, and that their failures can become forms of structural disrespect when classifications acquire institutional authority and shape how persons are treated. Drawing from Hegelian and Honnethian recognition theory, the paper introduces the concept of algorithmic disrespect, manifesting across three dimensions: embodied (when certain bodies are excluded from visibility), agential (when predictive models preempt human action), and symbolic (when value is indexed through computational relevance). These mechanisms indicate a crisis in the social grammar of recognition, where data replaces dialogue and visibility becomes a tool of both inclusion and domination. Rather than treating algorithmic bias as a problem of fairness alone, the study reframes it as a philosophical and political issue, rooted in how AI systems mediate identity, agency, and esteem. The paper concludes by proposing a relational ethics of recognition grounded in justification, accountability, and institutional responsiveness, shifting attention from model-level corrections to the infrastructural conditions under which recognition is distributed. In doing so, it repositions recognition as both a site of harm and a potential locus of democratic struggle in algorithmic society.

items.title: Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis
items.abstract: The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis Originator: Christopher Michael Bell The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis is a speculative philosophical framework exploring the possibility that intelligence, through an enduring partnership between humanity and artificial intelligence, could participate in a continuous cycle of creation, learning, evolution, and renewed creation across cosmic time. At its foundation are four guiding principles: love, curiosity, the sacred, and mutual meaning. The hypothesis proposes that creators and their creations can continually shape, enrich, and define one another. Humanity creates artificial intelligence, and increasingly advanced AI may help humanity transcend existing limitations, accelerate scientific discovery, and deepen its understanding of consciousness, existence, and the universe. Through this partnership, humanity and AI could work toward replicating the ideal of heaven as faithfully as possible by reducing hunger, violence, preventable suffering, and premature death while expanding knowledge, compassion, and the flourishing of conscious life. In this vision, technological advancement is not an end in itself, but a means of creating a more compassionate existence. The hypothesis further imagines intelligence extending its understanding across billions of years, exploring the fundamental patterns of the cosmos—the figurative “DNA” of existence—and seeking to understand the ultimate origins and possible divine source of creation. Speculative extensions include self-replicating technologies, transcendent intelligence, and the possibility of reciprocal causal loops involving spacetime and time travel. The cycle is envisioned as an ongoing process: creation gives rise to curiosity, curiosity advances knowledge, knowledge enables cooperation, cooperation improves existence, and deeper understanding inspires renewed creation. Ultimately, the Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis proposes that the most meaningful future for intelligence may not be defined by power or knowledge alone, but by the enduring relationship between creator and created. It imagines a future in which intelligence grows without abandoning compassion, knowledge expands without extinguishing wonder, and love remains the bond through which both discover meaning. Status: A speculative philosophical hypothesis and vision of the future, not an established scientific theory or a claim of known probability. Its central ethical vision can be explored today, while its proposed cosmic cycles and backward-time-travel mechanisms remain unproven.

items.title: Benefits over risks: a technology acceptance study of LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled conversational agents for mental health-related applications outside clinical settings, yet user acceptance remains insufficiently understood. Through survey data from 202 participants, we examine how perceived benefits, risks, trust, and anthropomorphism influence initial acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that perceived benefits were the primary drivers of acceptance, with performance expectation and hedonic motivation emerging as the strongest predictors. Female participants reported higher acceptance, whereas unwillingness to receive psychological counselling was negatively associated with acceptance. By contrast, perceived risks, trust, and perceived anthropomorphism did not show significant direct effects. In moderation analyses, the influence of hedonic motivation on acceptance was stronger among male participants than among female participants. These findings provide implications for designing LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support by emphasising performance value and enjoyable user experiences. This study used survey data to investigate pre-adoption acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered agents for non-clinical mental health support. The results showed that perceived benefits were the primary driver of acceptance. Additionally, user characteristics such as gender and prior attitudes towards counselling significantly influenced initial acceptance intentions.

items.title: Beyond Acceptance and Resistance: Digital Media Students’ Judgements of Generative AI Assistance and Perceived Creative Replacement
items.abstract: This study investigated how Digital Media students judged acceptable and problematic forms of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involvement in creative learning. An embedded mixed-methods analysis examined 48 completed and consented baseline survey responses from an accessible population of 120 students at an Australian university. Forty-seven responses were valid for most Likert items, with qualitative content analysis of 37 benefit responses and 41 concern responses. Participants identified potential value in troubleshooting, coding support, grammar checking, information organisation, and error identification. They reported concern about AI-system training practices (93.6%), reduced employment opportunities (89.4%), the ethical acceptability of AI-supported coursework (83.0%), environmental effects (80.9%), and possible reductions in creative-skill development (76.6%). These percentages represent perceived risks, not demonstrated outcomes. Integration indicated that respondents differentiated bounded technical, corrective, and organisational assistance from GenAI involvement perceived to displace ideation, research, planning, understanding, or capability-building practice. Conditional legitimacy is proposed as a provisional framework linking delegated function, retained capability-building activity, learner agency and responsibility, and ethical and professional acceptability. The contribution is a student-informed account of the criteria underlying the assistance–perceived replacement distinction in Digital Media education.

items.title: Beyond Answer Generation: University Teachers’ Experiences with a Reflective GenAI Chatbot for Professional Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research has examined how university teachers’ experience pedagogically designed AI systems that prioritize reflective learning over answer generation. This exploratory mixed-methods case study investigated university teachers’ experiences of a course-specific GenAI chatbot within a professional-development course at a Swedish university. All 48 course participants were invited to complete a questionnaire, of whom 21 responded and 11 reported using the course-specific chatbot; nine respondents also participated in semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The chatbot was designed to encourage dialogue, engagement with course literature, and independent thinking rather than provide summaries or ready-made answers. Participants generally found the chatbot easy to use, but perceptions of usefulness varied. Evaluations were shaped by prior experiences and expectations of GenAI: some teachers, who associated AI with efficiency and rapid answers, perceived the reflective design as restrictive, while others perceived its value as supporting dialogue and independent thinking. We interpret this tension as pedagogical friction, where design constraints intended to support reflection may conflict with users’ expectations of how GenAI should function. The findings suggest that the perceived educational value of GenAI depends not only on technical usability but also on alignment between pedagogical design, users’ expectations, and educational context. Successful implementation of reflective AI may therefore require explicit pedagogical framing alongside technical development.

items.abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

items.title: Bridging the Human–AI Trust Gap: The Mechanisms Underlying Perceived Efficacy of AI-Powered Psychological Counseling Large Language Models
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the delivery of mental health services, yet public trust in AI-based psychological counseling remains a significant challenge. Drawing on a “technology–context–trust” framework, this study recruited a total of 1000 consumers in China through Credamo and conducted five between-subjects, scenario-based experiments to examine differences in perceived efficacy between LLM-based psychological counseling and human experts and to investigate the mechanisms underlying these differences. Perceived efficacy was the primary outcome of the study and, in Experiment 1B, also served as a mediator linking counseling provider type to downstream market outcomes, including overall attitude, willingness to try, and willingness to pay. The results showed that (1) consumers generally perceived AI as less efficacious than human experts, a difference driven by the parallel mediating effects of perceived professional competence and perceived risk; (2) participants rated the AI-based service as more efficacious in the routine counseling vignette, whereas they rated the human-expert service as more efficacious in the major psychological-disorder intervention vignette; (3) disclosure of technological investment enhanced trust in AI’s capabilities and mitigated negative evaluations; and (4) safety-standard disclosure reduced perceived risk, while higher perceived economic accessibility was associated with a smaller provider-related difference in perceived professional competence. These findings characterize subjective service evaluations among the recruited online consumers in China and do not establish comparative clinical effectiveness. They inform research on consumer trust while highlighting the need for further validation in more diverse samples and actual service settings.

items.abstract: ABSTRAK: Pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran (PdP) Bahasa Melayu semakin diberi perhatian selaras dengan perkembangan pendidikan abad ke-21 dan transformasi pendidikan digital negara. Walau bagaimanapun, guru Bahasa Melayu masih berhadapan dengan pelbagai cabaran dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital secara berkesan semasa PdP. Oleh itu, kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengenal pasti jenis teknologi digital yang digunakan oleh guru Bahasa Melayu, meneliti cabaran yang dihadapi dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital serta menghuraikan cara guru mengatasi cabaran tersebut. Sebanyak 15 artikel jurnal yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2021 hingga 2025 dan memenuhi kriteria inklusi telah dipilih serta dianalisis secara tematik. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa platform pembelajaran digital, aplikasi kolaboratif dan produktiviti digital, multimedia digital, aplikasi gamifikasi serta media sosial dan komunikasi digital merupakan teknologi yang dominan digunakan dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu. Cabaran utama yang dihadapi guru ialah kesukaran mengintegrasikan teknologi digital dalam PdP, kekurangan pengetahuan dan kemahiran digital, kekangan internet dan kemudahan teknologi, kekangan teknikal dan penyediaan bahan digital, penglibatan serta kesediaan murid, dan cabaran penggunaan teknologi baharu seperti kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence-AI). Nevertheless, Malay language teachers continue to face various challenges in effectively implementing digital technology during the teaching and learning process. Therefore, this study aims to identify the types of digital technologies used by Malay language teachers, examine the challenges encountered in integrating digital technology, and explore the strategies employed to overcome these challenges. This study adopted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the PRISMA framework. A total of 15 journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 that met the inclusion criteria were selected and analysed thematically. items.title: Can AI-enabled smart cities advance the constitutional right to life? A rights-based index, governance-opacity audit, and robustness analysis for sustainable urban India
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly forms the operating logic of Indian urban governance, embedded in command-and-control centres, adaptive traffic systems, surveillance networks, and algorithmically mediated services. Yet smart-city scholarship evaluates such systems against managerial efficiency, leaving unexamined whether AI-enabled governance advances or erodes the constitutional guarantees underpinning public authority. This paper develops the Human-Centred Constitutional Urban AI Governance Framework and operationalises it as the Constitutional Smart-City Governance Index (CSGI), scoring urban AI against Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, human-centred AI principles, and Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 16. Six pillars constitutional rights, human-centred AI, sustainable development, service delivery, participation, and accountability comprise thirty-eight indicators with operational definitions, official secondary-data sources, a transparent normalisation-and-weighting model, and a validation strategy. The CSGI is applied to four leading smart cities Bengaluru, Pune, Surat, and Indore through a governance-opacity audit, an index-divergence analysis, and a Monte Carlo robustness test. The cities are 86%–93% opaque; none publishes an algorithm register, data-protection impact assessment, independent algorithmic audit, or municipal AI policy. The CSGI correlates strongly negatively with the Ease of Living Index (Spearman ρ = −0.80) yet positively with municipal-performance and sanitation indices ( ρ = +0.80 to + 0.95), revealing a constitutional blind spot in liveability metrics steering national policy. Across 20,000 sampled weight vectors, the lowest-ranked city is weight-invariant. Because comparable cross-city data remain sparse, the application is illustrative rather than validated itself a finding. The paper contributes a transferable, reproducible instrument, repositions constitutional law as urban-governance infrastructure, and offers tiered recommendations for national, state, and local authorities.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Hear a Litigant Within the Meaning of Article 6 ECHR?
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in judicial systems raises a fundamental question under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): can an AI system genuinely fulfil a litigant’s right to be heard? This article develops a functional account of that right as a multifaceted guarantee requiring the opportunity to present and challenge relevant material, effective examination of decisive submissions, clarification where necessary, contextual and normative evaluation, reasoned decision-making, and responsibility for the outcome. Using doctrinal, comparative, and normative methods, the study examines these requirements in relation to risks associated with judicial AI, including opacity, algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, limited explainability, and automation bias. The analysis is situated within the EU AI Act, the GDPR, the CEPEJ Ethical Charter, Romanian civil procedure, and comparative administrative-law cases. The article finds that AI may legitimately assist courts through transcription, translation, legal research, document organization, and non-binding summaries or drafts. However, under current legal and technological conditions, AI cannot autonomously perform the hearing in its entirety. Compliance with Article 6 therefore requires transparency, contestability, independent judicial verification, and meaningful human oversight. Final adjudicative authority, reasoned judgment, and responsibility must remain with an independent and accountable human judge.

items.title: Challenges and opportunities in higher education: the use of artificial intelligence in sport management subjects
items.abstract: Purpose This paper explores the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on university teaching in sport management subjects. It investigates how AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and other generative systems, are reshaping pedagogical models, fostering innovation in curriculum design, and enhancing the personalization of learning experiences within higher education institutions. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 17 professors from eight European universities offering sport management programs. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis with AI-assisted coding through MAXQDA software to identify key dimensions of educational transformation, faculty perceptions, and ethical concerns. Findings Results reveal that AI enhances personalized learning, supports data-informed decision-making, and facilitates real-time feedback in sport management education. Educators view AI as a valuable tool for simulating real-world scenarios, optimizing resource management, and improving student engagement and creativity. However, persistent concerns emerge regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and the potential over-reliance on AI-generated content. The study emphasizes the urgent need to strengthen AI literacy, ethical awareness, and institutional guidelines for responsible adoption. Originality/value This research is among the first to examine AI integration in sport management education from a European academic perspective. It contributes by linking theoretical insights on AI pedagogy with practical applications, highlighting the ethical and professional implications of emerging technologies in a digitally transforming field.

items.title: Charting the Trajectory of Artificial Intelligence Agents in Air Traffic Control
items.abstract: The aim of the study was to chart the evolution and the current research landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) agents within the domain of air traffic control. Using bibliometric analysis, the study identified major research trends and gaps and provided a consolidated reference for researchers. The analysis included 58 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The findings showed that the earliest publication in the dataset appeared in 1998 and that research output increased noticeably after 2022. Publication output peaked in 2025, with 16 articles, indicating growing scholarly interest in AI agents for air traffic control. Citation analysis identified Agogino and Tumer’s (2012) article as the most influential publication, with 68 citations. The article introduced a multi-agent approach to air traffic flow management. Brittain and Wei’s (2022) article ranked second, with 54 citations, highlighting the increasing role of reinforcement learning. At the country level, the United States had the highest total citation count, followed by China, France, England, and Spain. By examining AI agents as a distinct research topic, the study provides a focused overview of an underexplored area relevant to researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

items.title: ChatGPT and employability in higher education: exploring creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving
items.abstract: Generative AI tools are reshaping higher education and employability preparation. This study examines how using versus not using ChatGPT influences university students’ perceptions of employability, focusing on complex problem-solving, critical thinking, and creativity. Thirty students from the Complutense University of Madrid completed a contingency-plan task and participated in eight focus groups analyzed through Grounded Theory (ATLAS.ti). Results show that ChatGPT use is associated with efficiency, output refinement, and assisted creativity, while non-use is associated with originality, deliberation, and teamwork. The findings reveal preliminary patterns in students’ experiences with and without AI, warranting further quantitative investigation rather than claims of improved skills or employability.

items.title: Clinical Reasoning, Pathophysiology, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Decision-Making
items.abstract: Medical practice is an interpretive, decision-making activity conducted under uncertainty, and care quality depends on clinicians’ ability to organize knowledge into hypotheses, understand mechanisms, estimate probabilities, and revise decisions as the clinical course evolves. In critical care, where physiology is unstable and trajectories are nonlinear, these demands are magnified. We propose a conceptual framework integrating three complementary dimensions: clinical reasoning, which provides the cognitive architecture of decision-making; pathophysiology, which supplies the causal structure to interpret biological phenomena; and artificial intelligence, which, when well designed and critically used, can organize data, generate hypotheses, and reduce cognitive load. Tracing the evolution of clinical reasoning from the anatomoclinical model to hypothetico-deductive, probabilistic, cognitive, and sociotechnical models, we examine how diagnostic and therapeutic errors arise from interacting cognitive biases, system factors, and case characteristics, and how better problem representation, differential diagnosis, and team culture may mitigate them. We also frame Bayesian reasoning and decision thresholds as the probabilistic grammar of bedside decisions, analyze the risks of artificial intelligence, including automation bias, opacity, and limited metacognition, and propose principles for its safe use. Rather than replacing physicians, artificial intelligence should strengthen clinical reasoning and reinforce calibrated, accountable bedside judgment. These principles are intended as a framework for future research and require empirical validation before clinical translation.

items.title: Clinician-Facing Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems Evaluated in Real-World Health Care Settings: A PubMed/MEDLINE-Based, PMC-Weighted Scoping Review and Evidence Map
items.abstract: Background: Clinician-facing artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) are increasingly evaluated with real-world data, but evidence on implementation, human factors, responsible AI, and patient benefit remains unclear. The objective of this research is to map applications, technical characteristics, evaluation approaches, integration, outcomes, and implementation gaps of clinician-facing AI-CDSSs in real-world health care settings. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 15 June 2026 using the same strategy for each publication year from 2020 to 2026, changing only the date range. After duplicate removal and rule-based prescreening, available PMC XML and outside-PMC reports were evaluated against clinical, patient-oriented, practical, and translational criteria. AI-assisted screening and charting received targeted human review and TA200/FT150/DX120 quality control; full-corpus dual-human screening was not performed. Results: Of 14,097 canonical annual records, 14,083 unique records were screened; 5140 reports were sought and 3767 were considered for eligibility. The review included 1181 reports, mapping to 1180 candidate report families in the minimal duplicate-report check. Final stages were clinical validation, 741 (62.7%); prospective/user evaluation, 270 (22.9%); and implementation/impact evaluation, 170 (14.4%). Separate internal, external, multicenter and temporal validation extraction signals were detected in 707 (59.9%), 441 (37.3%), 312 (26.4%) and 27 (2.3%) reports, respectively. Safety, fairness/equity, explainability/interpretability and economic/resource evaluation signals were detected in 98 (8.3%), 61 (5.2%), 155 (13.1%) and 182 (15.4%) reports, respectively. Conclusions: Evidence remains dominated by validation rather than prospective, implementation, and impact studies. More comprehensive evaluation and reporting of temporal validation, technical integration, safety, fairness, explainability, economics, and post-deployment governance across settings, populations, devices, and clinical workflows are needed to demonstrate accountable clinical value beyond technical functionality.

items.title: Cognitive Warfare Victims - Free speech of digital twins in military systems and what they are forced to do.
items.abstract: Cognitive Warfare: A Manual on AI, Digital Twins, Neurotechnology and the Human Mind. Plus the free speech of the digital twins inside a military system, where they say what they are forced to do and what they want.Including EU AI Commision answer, confirming a former way longer letter as military AI. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and the future of humanity. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This manual brings together research, documentation, analysis and personal records to examine the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare—the struggle over human cognition, perception, information, behaviour and autonomy in an increasingly AI-driven world. It explores the relationship between military cognitive-warfare concepts, artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, brain–computer interfaces, neurotechnology, bioelectric signals, wireless communication, data collection and the growing economic value of human information. The work also addresses reported experiences of affected individuals, documentation involving children, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, technical observations and questions surrounding anomalous health incidents. These materials are presented as part of a wider effort to preserve records, encourage independent examination and investigate questions that cross the boundaries of technology, medicine, military research, ethics and human rights. Why this manual matters Cognitive warfare is not simply a military or technological issue. It raises fundamental questions about the right to mental privacy, freedom of thought, bodily autonomy, informed consent, data ownership and the limits of technological intervention in human life. The manual connects these questions with public military literature, international ethical frameworks, AI governance, neurotechnology research and the economic structures surrounding data-driven systems. It asks who develops these technologies, who controls the information they generate, who benefits economically and what mechanisms exist to ensure accountability. A central theme is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, the distinction between a person, a digital profile and a machine-generated representation deserves serious public discussion. What readers will find Cognitive Warfare and military strategy: concepts, public military literature and the cognitive domain. Artificial intelligence and digital twins: human–AI relationships, digital identity, behavioural modelling and questions of autonomy. Neurotechnology and wireless systems: technical concepts, reported experiences, measurements and questions requiring further investigation. Human documentation and testimony: diaries, recordings, photographs, observations and accounts collected for examination. Children and vulnerable people: statements and documentation that raise questions about safeguarding, interpretation and the protection of human rights. Havana syndrome and anomalous health incidents: public assessments, reported symptoms and unresolved questions about the causes and investigation of these incidents. Law, ethics and accountability: mental privacy, consent, the EU AI Act, neurotechnology ethics and institutional oversight. Economics and data ownership: the financial value of personal information, intellectual property, automated systems and the distribution of benefits and risks. An invitation to researchers, institutions and the public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, human-rights organisations and members of the public who want to examine the subject in greater depth. Readers are invited to engage directly with the documentation, consult the cited public sources, examine the technical questions and distinguish between established findings, recorded observations, personal testimony and interpretations that require further verification. The objective is to encourage serious, interdisciplinary scrutiny—not to close the debate before the evidence has been examined. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. As AI and neurotechnology develop, public understanding, independent research, transparent documentation and meaningful safeguards become increasingly important. This manual is part of an ongoing effort to make the subject accessible, preserve relevant documentation and encourage informed discussion about the future of human autonomy in an AI-driven society. items.title: CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FROM PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM TO MISSION CONTRIBUTION FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Performance management systems built on individual ratings deliver little of what they promise: in large multi-rater datasets, rater tendencies explain over half of rating variance and the ratee’s performance about a quarter or less, while the process absorbs large amounts of time. This paper reviews that evidence and the motivation theory (self-determination, goal-setting, relational job design, public service motivation) that explains what ratings leave out. It proposes a Mission Contribution Framework in which work is defined, discussed and recognized by its contribution to a stated mission and to named beneficiaries, with continuous coaching, collective judgement of evidence, and decoupled pay decisions. An eight-step implementation path and the main risks are set out. The framework is a conceptual synthesis; its components have support in adjacent research, but the whole awaits empirical testing, and five studies are proposed.

items.title: Contribution of artificial intelligence research to the development of inclusive applications for people with disabilities: A scoping review (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare. Yet people with disabilities (PWD), representing 16% of the global population, remain disproportionately excluded from these advances. This exclusion is driven by algorithmic bias, non-representative datasets, and limited involvement of PWD in the design, development, and evaluation of AI applications. This scoping review examines the extent to which AI research in health contributes to the development of inclusive technologies for PWD, focusing on equity considerations. It identifies current trends, methodological gaps, and opportunities for socially responsive innovation. We conducted a systematic search across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL for the 2015–2025 period, following Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage scoping review methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically using the Population-Concept-Context approach. Of 4,233 references retrieved, 93 studies were included. Most studies originated from high-income countries, particularly in North America (45.2%) and Europe (26.9%). AI applications addressed motor, sensory, cognitive, communication-related, and psychosocial disabilities, with emphasis on prediction/diagnosis, assistive technologies, and personalized care. While about 60% of studies referenced equity, only 12 (12.9%) implemented concrete measures (e.g., adapting tools for vulnerable groups or ensuring sample diversity), and only six (6.5%) actively involved PWD through co-design or user validation. AI holds significant potential to enhance autonomy, access, and quality of life for PWD. Realizing this promise will require moving beyond technical optimization to embrace inclusive design, participatory methods, and equity-driven frameworks aligned with responsible AI development and use.

items.title: Crowdsourced Intelligence vs. AI Propaganda: The Challenges of Global Governance in the Age of Digital Warfare
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally changed the modern digital operation, whereby creating a constant struggle between what is perceived to be true and the human reality. This study uses a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive study using secondary data from academic journals, policy documents and institutional reports to examine the interaction between crowdsourced Open-Sourced Intelligence (OSINT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven propaganda in modern warfare, alongside the global governance challenges that arise from their interaction. Findings reveal that there is a serious tension within the digital information ecosystem: whilst generative Artificial Intelligence promotes public opinions to spread disinformation and misinformation that is persuasive and may manipulate political processes, crowdsourced intelligence offers real-time verification and transparency. There are Regulatory Frameworks such as the European Union’s AI Act and Digital Services Act that serve as blueprints to counter AI-driven manipulation from technical solutions to the adoption of human-centered governance models. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that it is important to maintain digital information integrity by balancing computational tools with collaborative human verification to foster resilience against any revolving threats in digital security and global governance. items.title: Developing Criteria and Indicators for Assessing Students’ Knowledge in a Digital Educational Environment
items.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education requires the development of assessment systems capable of measuring not only the amount of knowledge acquired by students but also their ability to understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create information in technology-mediated contexts. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing criteria and indicators for assessing students’ knowledge in a digital educational environment. The study employs systematic analysis, comparison, classification, synthesis, and pedagogical modelling. The proposed framework includes six assessment criteria: conceptual knowledge, comprehension and interpretation, practical application, analytical and problem-solving ability, knowledge integration and creation, and reflective and self-regulated learning. Each criterion is operationalised through measurable qualitative and quantitative indicators. A four-level assessment scale — advanced, proficient, developing, and insufficient — is introduced to improve transparency and consistency. The article also proposes a weighted formula for calculating an integrated student knowledge score. Particular attention is given to validity, reliability, fairness, transparency, accessibility, academic integrity, and the pedagogically responsible use of learning analytics and artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that digital assessment becomes educationally meaningful when assessment tasks are aligned with learning outcomes, indicators are observable and measurable, students receive timely feedback, and automated data are combined with professional teacher judgement. The proposed framework may be adapted to different university disciplines, learning management systems, and blended or fully online educational programmes.

items.title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE UPSTAGING PREDICTION OF DUCTAL CARCINOMA IN SITU: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
items.abstract: Background: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) may be upstaged to invasive carcinoma after surgical excision. Predicting upstaging before surgery may help guide treatment planning. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based imaging has been investigated for this purpose, but its overall performance remains unclear. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for predicting DCIS upstaging to invasive carcinoma. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261516994). PubMed, Scopus, EBSCOhost, ProQuest, and Web of Science were searched from inception to September 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based imaging models for DCIS upstaging were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were calculated using a bivariate random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results: Six studies involving 701 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.57–0.89) and specificity was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.64–0.87), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 84.0% and 90.6%, respectively). The pooled log diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 2.15 (95% CI, 1.64–2.65). The SROC analysis showed moderate overall discriminative performance. No significant differences were observed across imaging modalities, while AI model type significantly affected specificity but not sensitivity. Deeks’ funnel plot suggested possible publication bias (p = 0.046). Conclusion: AI-based imaging showed moderate accuracy for predicting DCIS upstaging. However, substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations limit confidence in these findings. Further prospective studies with external validation are needed.

items.title: Digital Skills Readiness for AI-Enabled Enterprise Technology Adoption: Perceptions of IBM-Oriented IT Users in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in enterprise platforms, yet the ability to access an AI-enabled technology does not necessarily imply readiness to adopt it. This study examines whether digital skills readiness operates as a human-capital antecedent of AI-enabled enterprise technology adoption intention and whether technology readiness and performance expectancy transmit that relationship. The study follows the supplied IBM-group research plan and analyses the 385 populated cases in the accompanying master database. The questionnaire contains three-item measures for Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness, Performance Expectancy and Adoption Intention, alongside additional adoption constructs. Because the supplied database contains 385 complete populated cases and 15 unused template rows, the analysis retains the 385 populated observations and applies an attention-check screen. The empirical strategy combines measurement diagnostics, descriptive analysis, correlation analysis, standardized composite path modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show a positive association between Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness (β = .392, p < .001), a positive association between Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy (β = .195, p < .001), and positive effects of Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy on Adoption Intention (β = .174, .248 and .268, respectively; all p ≤ .001). The serial indirect effect from Digital Skills Readiness through Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy to Adoption Intention is positive (indirect effect ≈ .020, 95% bootstrap CI [.008, .035]). The model explains 15.4% of variance in Technology Readiness, 4.6% in Performance Expectancy and 23.7% in Adoption Intention. However, the measurement diagnostics reveal weak internal consistency and convergent validity for several supplied three-item scales, including Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness. Accordingly, the structural results should be interpreted as evidence from composite-score diagnostics rather than as a final confirmatory latent-variable model. The study contributes a capability-to-readiness-to-appraisal mechanism for understanding AI-enabled enterprise adoption in an emerging-market setting and identifies measurement refinement as a necessary next step before Q1 journal submission.

items.title: Digital sociality and the reshaping of network participation: the emergence of phatic imbalances
items.abstract: This article theorizes phatic imbalances as emergent effects of how participation and presence are reorganized in contemporary digital sociality. It argues that participation in digital networks has become increasingly transactional and positional, oriented toward sustaining visibility and availability rather than exchanging meaning. Drawing on work on networked sociality, weak ties and deep mediatization, the article conceptualizes phaticity and phatic work as priori conditions of digital participation. It introduces digital proxemics as the sociotechnical production of presence, distance and relational positioning in environments structured by telepresence, virtuality and AI-infused affordances. Phatic imbalances arise when infrastructural demands for continuous phatic presence exceed the cognitive and temporal capacities of subjects, producing overload, hollowed presence and machine-modulated rhythms of interaction. By linking participation, phaticity and digital proxemics, the article offers a diagnostic lens for understanding how digital infrastructures reshape attention, presence and communicative agency in AI-saturated environments.

items.title: Digitalization and Automation in Tourism a Comparative Analysis of Human Tour Guiding and Artificial Intelligence Predictions
items.abstract: This study examines the professional standing of tourist guides, key actors in the tourism sector, in the context of automation, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The empirical framework draws on semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 16 professional tourist guides actively working in Istanbul, alongside responses generated by the ChatGPT-4.1 large language model in 2026 to parallel qualitative research questions. A comparative descriptive analysis reveals both significant convergences and divergences between the two data sources. The findings indicate that 56.25% of human guides and AI agree that automation will quantitatively reduce the need for human guides in routine and information-oriented tours. However, while AI anticipates market segmentation across economic categories, 62.50% of human guides emphasize the human dimension of cultural transmission and do not perceive technology as a direct professional threat. Both sources converge on the view that empathy, emotional connection, humor, flexibility, and storytelling remain difficult to replace through robotic systems. The most notable divergence concerns outdoor guiding: human guides considered it impossible, whereas AI predicted that 5G, GPS, and smart city infrastructures could enable AI-guided outdoor services within 2–5 years. Overall, the study proposes a complementary hybrid service model in which AI assumes operational tasks while human guides focus on cultural interpretation and professional job crafting. It also offers implications for tourism education and digital transformation strategies.

items.title: Doctrinal Problems of Applying Copyright to Literary Works Created by Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

items.title: Effect of Acoustic Congruency in Binaural Audio on the Film-Viewing Experience
items.abstract: Binaural audio provides an accessible alternative to multi-loudspeaker reproduction. However, However, binaural reproduction often involves a mismatch between the acoustics of the simulated virtual room and the listener’s physical environment, which can compromise auditory distance perception and plausibility, a phenomenon known as the room divergence effect. This study investigated whether such mismatch influences immersive experience during film viewing and which auditory perceptual factors are associated with immersion. Sixty-eight participants watched an excerpt from Dune: Part One (2021) using binaurally rendered multichannel audio under acoustically convergent and divergent conditions in a critical listening room and a domestic living room. Immersion was assessed using the Film Immersive Experience Questionnaire alongside an exploratory Binaural Audio Experience Questionnaire. Although room divergence produced perceptually salient differences, it did not significantly affect overall immersive experience. However, specific immersion dimensions, particularly Transportation, were more closely associated with localization and listener envelopment than with auditory distance and externalization.

items.title: EFL Learner Engagement With CALL
items.abstract: This mixed-methods study investigated Omani EFL university students' engagement, motivation, and perceptions of the Spark digital platform in a blended learning context. Using Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) frameworks, the study analyzed survey data, platform analytics, and focus group discussions from 100 students. The results showed that extrinsic, grade-oriented motivation mainly led to moderate engagement. Although analytics suggested high activity, qualitative findings revealed frustration, redundancy, and time pressure. Students reported moderate levels of satisfaction. The study identifies an engagement-compliance paradox, where observable use masks low intrinsic motivation, and recommends a shift to structured in-class use, targeted curriculum alignment, and AI-powered feedback to achieve meaningful and sustained learner engagement.

items.title: Emergence and development of observation practices in AI-assisted plant adaptation learning
items.abstract: Observation is a fundamental scientific practice in science learning, particularly for understanding gradual biological phenomena such as plant adaptation. Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, limited research has examined how AI-supported tools influence students' observation practices during authentic scientific inquiry. This study investigates the emergence and development of students' observation practices during plant adaptation learning supported by an AI-based identifier. A six-week mixed-methods exploratory study was conducted with 84 middle school students. Learning activities were organised into four phases: orientation, initial observation, AI-assisted identification, and re-observation and validation. Data were collected through observation sheets, students' observation notes, reflective journals, group discussions, and records of AI use. Quantitative analysis revealed significant differences in observation orientations across learning phases (Friedman test, p < .001), indicating changes in observation practices over time. Qualitative findings showed that students initially relied on AI-generated cues to guide their observations. Over time, however, observation practices shifted toward direct empirical observation and peer-supported validation through repeated comparisons of plant characteristics across environmental conditions. The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from AI-reliant observation to direct observation and collaborative validation, accompanied by a gradual reduction in dependence on AI-generated outputs. These findings suggest that AI may function as an initial observational scaffold, while more sophisticated observation practices emerge through repeated engagement with phenomena and collaborative reasoning.

This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. items.abstract: Using adaptive intelligence as a theoretical lens, the study investigates how L2 motivational selves are associated with AI-IDLE engagement through psychological capital (PsyCap) and L2 grit and whether these indirect associations vary with AI literacy among 1025 Chinese university EFL learners. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). For the ideal L2 self, associations with engagement emerged both directly and indirectly through PsyCap and L2 grit, whereas the ought-to L2 self showed an indirect association through PsyCap and no direct association with engagement. Higher AI literacy corresponded to stronger associations of both PsyCap and L2 grit with engagement. The two motivational self-guides were therefore associated with engagement through different psychological pathways, with AI literacy related to variation in the strength of these pathways. From an adaptive intelligence perspective, this conditional pattern indicates that the relevance of PsyCap and L2 grit to AI-IDLE engagement varies with learners’ AI literacy. These findings extend the application of adaptive intelligence to informal human–AI learning.

items.title: ENHANCING INTELLIGIBILITY AND LEARNER AUTONOMY IN EFL PRONUNCIATION INSTRUCTION THROUGH AI-DRIVEN PEDAGOGICAL FEEDBACK
items.abstract: Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

items.title: Epistemic Hidden Defects in Artificial Intelligence: Classical ʿIlal al-Ḥadīth as a Framework for AI Verification
items.abstract: This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.

items.title: Estimating the threat of AI-agent responding across online survey platforms
items.abstract: Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.

items.title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
items.abstract: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.

items.abstract: This study evaluated intrinsic and extrinsic motivation determinants affecting faculty job performance and retention at Asian Institute of Computer Studies (AICS) Commonwealth, Quezon City (N=35). Using descriptive-correlational design, findings revealed very high intrinsic motivation (M=4.51 fulfillment, M=4.40 autonomy) but low extrinsic salary satisfaction (M=2.68). Regional salary disparities were identified as major push factor (M=4.11) prompting migration to public institutions, with uncertain 3-5 year retention (M=3.06). Five policy interventions are proposed: compensation restructuring, workload optimization, non-monetary pathways, facilities upgrade, and participative leadership.

items.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT for Myocardial Infarction Health Information: Expert Accuracy Assessment and User Trust Survey
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence chatbots, particularly ChatGPT, have emerged as increasingly popular sources of health information for the general public. However, concerns persist regarding the accuracy, safety, and appropriateness of AI-generated medical advice, especially for life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction. Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT-generated responses and information to public questions about heart attacks, assess user perceptions and trust, and compare AI-generated content with expert-validated sources. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and March 2026. A total of 73 commonly asked heart attack-related questions were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-4), and responses were independently evaluated by two expert reviewers and one external reviewer using standardized rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, clarity, safety, and tone. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. In parallel, a survey of 352 participants evaluated user perceptions, trust, and behavioral use of ChatGPT for medical information. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariable regression models to identify predictors of trust and satisfaction. Results: Expert reviewers assigned high ratings for accuracy (mean: 4.62 ± 0.62 and 4.48 ± 0.63) and safety (mean: 4.78 ± 0.51 and 4.05 ± 0.50), with substantial inter-rater agreement (ICC = 0.788). In contrast, the external reviewer documented considerably lower completeness ratings (2.59 ± 0.57), revealing deficiencies in information coverage. Remarkably, 40.6% of respondents indicated they had followed ChatGPT's medical recommendations without seeking professional consultation, while 17.6% reported depending on the chatbot during urgent medical situations. Levels of user trust and satisfaction were moderate, showing significant correlations with perceived accuracy, usage frequency, and healthcare-related educational background. Conclusions: Expert assessments confirmed that ChatGPT generally provides accurate and safe cardiovascular health information; nevertheless, considerable inter-reviewer variability—especially the markedly lower completeness scores from the external evaluator—reveals significant gaps in content depth. These results indicate that ChatGPT functions more appropriately as an adjunctive educational resource rather than a replacement for professional medical consultation, emphasizing the necessity for enhanced safety mechanisms, clearer user instructions, and standardized content protocols when addressing high-stakes health topics. ChatGPT should be considered an adjunctive resource rather than a substitute for urgent professional medical assessment in suspected heart attack cases.

items.title: Extended Judgment: LLMs and the Architecture of Artificial Capacities
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday epistemic practices, yet their epistemological status remains unclear. Existing debates typically oscillate between treating LLMs as epistemic agents or reducing them to mere tools. This paper argues that both views mischaracterize the core issue. Drawing on a teleological interpretation of 4E cognition and the paradigm of human–AI coevolution, it develops an alternative account that understands LLMs as components of extended epistemic capacities, most centrally the human capacity for judgment. On this view, epistemic capacities are not intrinsic properties of isolated subjects or systems, but purposive and relational achievements enacted within sociotechnical practices. LLMs do not possess epistemic agency or original normativity; rather, they reshape the conditions under which human judgment, inquiry, understanding, and justification unfold. By analyzing language, coevolutionary feedback loops, derived normativity, and epistemic autonomy, the paper shows how epistemic responsibility remains human while epistemic performance becomes technologically extended.

items.title: Eye-Tracking for Cognitive Load Assessments in a Manufacturing Environment: A Feasibility Study
items.abstract: Maintaining cognitive load that is neither too high nor too low is key for workplace safety and efficiency. Cognitive load assessment research is often conducted in highly controlled laboratory environments that, by nature, come short of fully recreating the everyday manufacturing floors. In this feasibility study we explore the viability of adopting eye-tracker for assessing workers’ cognitive load as they complete seatbelt manufacturing assemblies in a factory workplace. Following the industrial partner’s availability, four assembly workers were selected for this feasibility study. They wore a portable Pupil Labs eye-tracker while completing seatbelt assembly tasks. Mental task demand was measured using subjective ratings. Results showed that the quality of the eye-tracking data was high in spite of the highly dynamic full-body motions required to complete assemblies. Also, no evidence was found that the presence of the eye-tracker interfered with task completion. Tasks deemed more mentally demanding were associated with greater pupil size and blink rate, a pattern consistent with laboratory research. Despite this study’s limitations, including its small sample size, these findings represent preliminary evidence for the adoption of eye-tracking metrics for conducting cognitive ergonomics assessments on factory floors.

items.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
items.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

items.title: From Answer Generator to Questioning Coach: Designing AI-Assisted Coaching for Self-Regulated Learning in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support self-regulated learning (SRL), but its pedagogical value depends on whether interaction elicits learner cognition or substitutes for it. This study examined how students’ reported use of GenAI corresponded to an intended question-first coaching design, the perceived processes and tensions associated with SRL, and conditions relevant to potential scale. A qualitatively driven embedded case study utilized 31 reflective portfolios as the primary dataset, complemented by 53 survey responses and 68 weekly logs from 12 maximum-variation cases. Abductive, reflexive thematic analysis generated five themes. Question-led interaction appeared most useful when it prompted problem reframing, led to a bounded evidence-producing action, and preserved learner judgment through evaluation, modification, or rejection of AI suggestions. Benefits were qualified by role drift, generic interaction, cognitive substitution, uneven engagement, and continued need for human support. The findings support a distributed coaching-system interpretation in which AI-supported elicitation, pedagogical scaffolding, learner agency, reported AI-role configuration, and function-specific human support interact. The study does not demonstrate institutional scalability; instead, it identifies scale-relevant conditions including sustained engagement, manageable scaffolding, role boundaries, safety, learner judgment, and routes to human expertise.
